actions.justification: Patient presents with ankle swelling and dyspnea — assessing volume status (JVD, peripheral edema, lung crackles) is the first step to classify hemodynamic profile (wet vs dry) and guide diuretic therapy.
Concurrent perfusion assessment (skin temperature, capillary refill, pulse pressure) is essential to differentiate warm vs cold profile, determining whether to use diuretics alone or add inotropes.
BNP/NT-proBNP is a key biomarker to confirm heart failure diagnosis, assess severity, and guide treatment decisions per AHF guidelines.
Chest X-ray is essential to assess for pulmonary edema, cardiomegaly, and pleural effusions in acute heart failure presentation.
Basic metabolic panel needed to assess renal function and electrolytes before initiating IV diuretic therapy (furosemide), and to establish baseline creatinine/potassium.
Patient is WET and WARM (congested with good perfusion, MAP 114). IV furosemide is first-line treatment for acute decompensated heart failure with volume overload (ankle swelling, dyspnea, SpO2 95%).

Echocardiogram is essential to assess ejection fraction and wall motion in this heart failure patient, guiding further management decisions (HFrEF vs HFpEF). Patient has HTN, DM, and AF which increase likelihood of structural abnormalities.
Troponin should be ordered to rule out acute coronary syndrome as a precipitant of decompensated heart failure, particularly given the comorbidities of HTN and DM2.

Cardiology consultation is warranted for this patient with decompensated heart failure and multiple comorbidities (HTN, DM2, AF, obesity) to optimize management strategy and consider further workup or advanced therapies.

Patient is WET and WARM (congested with adequate perfusion, BP 158/92, SpO2 95%). With hypertension and signs of volume overload, a vasodilator (e.g., nitroglycerin or nitroprusside) is indicated to reduce afterload and preload, improve symptoms, and help manage elevated BP in acute decompensated heart failure alongside diuresis already initiated.

Patient has heart failure with SpO2 95% and elevated BP. Prior perfusion assessment completed; if cardiogenic shock features are present (cold/wet profile), inotropic support may be indicated. This is the only remaining available action and warrants consideration given the clinical context of acute decompensated heart failure with atrial fibrillation and multiple comorbidities.
Mandatory action not yet completed. Detailed history is essential to characterize onset, duration, precipitating factors, medication adherence, and functional class of this heart failure patient.
Mandatory action not yet completed. Physical exam to assess JVD, S3 gallop, crackles, peripheral edema severity, and signs of poor perfusion is critical in acute heart failure management.

Mandatory action not yet completed. ECG is essential given this patient's atrial fibrillation comorbidity to assess rate, rhythm, and identify any ischemic changes or arrhythmias contributing to decompensation.
Mandatory action - assess renal function, electrolytes, and glucose, critical in a patient with hypertension, diabetes, and heart failure on diuretic therapy.
Mandatory action - BNP/NT-proBNP is essential to confirm acute heart failure diagnosis and guide severity assessment and treatment response.
Mandatory action - chest X-ray to evaluate for pulmonary edema, cardiomegaly, and pleural effusions to characterize the degree of congestion.

Mandatory action: CBC is required to assess for anemia (which can exacerbate heart failure and dyspnea), infection, and baseline hematologic status in this patient with HF, atrial fibrillation, and diabetes.

Mandatory action: TSH is required to rule out thyroid dysfunction (hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism) as a contributing or precipitating cause of heart failure and atrial fibrillation in this patient.

Patient has hypertension (BP 158/92), SpO2 95%, and is on diuresis — assessing hemodynamic profile (wet/warm vs wet/cold) guides further management decisions including vasodilator titration and need for ICU escalation.
Echo has been ordered; assessing LVEF is critical to classify HFrEF vs HFpEF and guide evidence-based therapy selection (ACEi/ARB, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i dosing, device therapy candidacy).

Patient's BP remains elevated at 158/92 mmHg despite prior vasodilator administration. Additional vasodilator therapy is indicated to reduce afterload and improve cardiac output in this hypertensive, congested patient.

Patient has known atrial fibrillation and heart failure; once LVEF is established, ICD candidacy should be evaluated per guideline recommendations for sudden cardiac death prevention in HF patients with reduced EF.

Assessing NYHA functional class is essential to guide HF management decisions, medication titration, and eligibility for device therapies. Patient has exertional dyspnea and ankle swelling suggesting at least NYHA Class II-III.
Patient has heart failure with atrial fibrillation. CRT (cardiac resynchronization therapy) indication should be assessed based on LVEF, QRS duration, and NYHA class per ESC/ACC guidelines.
Patient remains congested (ankle swelling, exertional dyspnea, SpO2 95%). Additional diuretic therapy may be needed to achieve euvolemia, especially given obesity which may affect diuretic response.

Assessing structural abnormalities (valvular disease, wall motion, chamber size) is important to guide ongoing heart failure management and identify treatable causes, especially given the patient's history of hypertension and atrial fibrillation.

With multiple comorbidities (hypertension, diabetes, AFib, obesity) and heart failure, ensuring guideline-directed medical therapy is optimized is critical for long-term outcomes and informs the treatment plan.

Evaluating whether this patient may need advanced therapies (CRT, ICD beyond initial assessment, mechanical support) is appropriate at this stage of evaluation, particularly given the complexity of the case.

Patient has HFrEF with hypertension, diabetes, and atrial fibrillation. Confirming that guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) is optimized is the next priority after initial stabilization, diuresis, and vasodilation have been initiated.

Patient has hypertension and heart failure. ACE inhibitor, ARB, or ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) is a cornerstone of GDMT for heart failure to reduce mortality and hospitalizations, and should be initiated or confirmed if not already on therapy.

Beta-blocker therapy (e.g., carvedilol, metoprolol succinate) is indicated for heart failure management and also helps control rate in atrial fibrillation. Should be initiated once patient is euvolemic and hemodynamically stable.

Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (e.g., spironolactone/eplerenone) is part of guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure and helps with volume management and neurohormonal blockade, especially relevant given this patient's persistent congestion and hypertension.

Patient has ongoing signs of congestion (dyspnea, ankle swelling, SpO2 95%). If response to IV furosemide is inadequate, adding a thiazide-type diuretic (combination diuresis) can enhance diuretic efficacy in resistant congestion.

Cardiac rehabilitation is recommended for heart failure patients to improve functional capacity, quality of life, and outcomes. Patient has multiple comorbidities (obesity, diabetes, hypertension, AF) that would benefit from structured rehabilitation.

Patient has heart failure with atrial fibrillation and is hemodynamically stable (BP 158/92, HR 78). Continuing beta blocker therapy is appropriate for rate control in AF and as GDMT for heart failure, provided no contraindications.
